video_title: The People Who’ve Survived Collapse | with Victoria Sweet | TGS 243
gist: Nate Hagens interviews Victoria Sweet, founder of the Ishkode Fund, who argues that Indigenous-led groups (receiving only ~0.25% of US philanthropic dollars) hold ecological, governance and resilience knowledge needed for coming collapse, and that donors should deploy capital now with venture-like risk tolerance. Market relevance is low; the main hard signals are the Copper River salmon failure and Hagens' remark that Hormuz-driven price spikes have not yet fully hit North America.

insights.claim: Indigenous-led organizations receive only about one quarter of 1% of US philanthropic dollars, despite Indigenous peoples being roughly 3-7% of the population, leaving a large structural funding gap that the Ishkode Fund (supporting ~200 groups) aims to close.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Impact/ESG allocators looking for underfunded, high-leverage grant categories can treat Indigenous-led groups as a neglected niche with low competition for capital.
insights.quote: despite indigenous-led organizations receiving only one quarter of 1% of philanthropic dollars in the United States

insights.claim: Philanthropy can function as first-loss or seed capital inside a broader capital stack, funding things investors will not touch because it does not require guarantees.
insights.speaker: Victoria Sweet
insights.so_what: Blended-finance structures can use grant dollars to de-risk projects that later attract investment capital.
insights.quote: It can seed fund something where an investor says, "Well, we have to have certain, uh, guarantees to back it." A philanthropist doesn't have to do that.

insights.claim: Philanthropists apply stricter due diligence to small Indigenous nonprofits than venture capitalists apply to multimillion-dollar risky bets, and a single Indigenous project failure is used to justify withholding funding from the whole category, a double standard not applied to other 501(c)(3)s.
insights.speaker: Victoria Sweet
insights.so_what: Mispriced risk perception suggests outsized social return per dollar for donors willing to accept venture-style risk in grantmaking.
insights.quote: You put these little nonprofits through greater due diligence and proofs than they put these massive investment opportunities

insights.claim: US donors often redirect Indigenous funding to the Global South on the assumption that US tribes are well funded via casinos, treaty rights and tax benefits, causing domestic tribes to be overlooked.
insights.speaker: Victoria Sweet
insights.so_what: Domestic tribal communities may be a more neglected and therefore higher-marginal-impact funding target than international Indigenous programs.

insights.claim: Speed matters: Sweet argues capital should be deployed now rather than parked in vehicles awaiting the perfect project, using money while it 'still has the value that it has' ahead of anticipated systemic disruption.
insights.speaker: Victoria Sweet
insights.so_what: Signals pressure on foundations and DAFs to raise payout rates and accelerate deployment in a crisis-oriented giving environment.
insights.quote: We're past the time where we should just keep our money sitting in these different vehicles waiting for the proper moment to release it

insights.claim: Intermediaries fluent in both Western systems and Indigenous communities can route donor money by theme (e.g., midwifery, regenerative agriculture) and reduce the unintentional harm that keeps cautious funders from giving.
insights.speaker: Victoria Sweet
insights.so_what: Intermediary funds lower transaction and knowledge costs, a model for donors lacking in-house expertise.

insights.claim: Most tribal casinos are not highly profitable; wealthy per-capita gaming tribes are the exception, and casinos arose as one of the only economic tools available to tribes placed on poor land and kept in a government commodity-dependency model.
insights.speaker: Victoria Sweet
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate the economics of a few large gaming tribes to tribal economies broadly; most tribal gaming revenue is small and funds basic services.
insights.quote: The majority of tribes are not incredibly wealthy because of their casinos.

insights.claim: On Sweet's tribe's land, casino revenue funds elder food, early childhood education, roads and second-chance jobs for formerly incarcerated members rather than large per-capita payouts.
insights.speaker: Victoria Sweet
insights.so_what: Tribal gaming revenue in many cases functions as a substitute for public services, not as surplus wealth.

themes.theme: Traditional ecological knowledge as climate-adaptation signal

insights.claim: A Cordova, Alaska elder predicted years in advance that salmon would leave the Copper River within five to eight years; this year three of the five salmon species did not return, and he is now shifting to kelp planting as a bridge food source.
insights.speaker: Victoria Sweet
insights.so_what: Copper River salmon disruption is a watch item for Alaska fisheries and seafood supply; kelp/seaweed cultivation emerges as a local adaptation play.
insights.quote: This year, for the first time in his lifetime, three of the five species of salmon did not return to the Copper River.

insights.claim: Indigenous place names and oral traditions encode historical climate events; a Zuni community found water during a drought by digging at a location whose name contained the word for water.
insights.speaker: Victoria Sweet
insights.so_what: Local traditional knowledge can be a low-cost input for water and climate-resilience projects.

insights.claim: Exclusionary conservation (keep humans out) can backfire: on a Hawaiian taro farm, active removal of invasive grasses let an endangered ground-nesting bird recover to about 40 of the remaining ~400, even though regulators wanted all work halted.
insights.speaker: Victoria Sweet
insights.so_what: Stewardship-based (active management) conservation models may outperform protected-area exclusion models, relevant to land, biodiversity-credit and conservation finance design.
insights.quote: of the 400 of these birds still in existence, 40 of them were spotted on this area of land

insights.claim: Pairing Indigenous elders with Western scientists (satellite data, studies) fills mutual knowledge gaps, and Hagens argues regenerative agriculture and living-systems restoration cannot succeed without Indigenous input.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Regenerative-ag and nature-based projects that integrate Indigenous partners may gain legitimacy and effectiveness.

insights.claim: Wisdom as restraint: harvesting practices of never taking everything contrast with the Western extract-until-depleted-then-move-on model.
insights.speaker: Victoria Sweet
insights.so_what: A framing for sustainable-yield resource management versus extractive depletion business models.
insights.quote: You don't grab every berry. You leave something behind for the birds

insights.claim: Hagens expects philanthropy to face huge demand as communities enter dire need, noting that price spikes from the Hormuz situation have hit Asia harder than North America so far.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Implies energy-price shock transmission to North America may still be ahead; watch for lagged inflation and rising social-service demand.
insights.quote: I don't think the real price, uh, um, spikes from the Hormuz situation have hit North America as much as they have in Asia.

insights.claim: Sweet frames US governmental systems as collapsing and argues the Haudenosaunee influenced the US Constitution but key pieces, notably women's leadership, were left out, reducing its effectiveness.
insights.speaker: Victoria Sweet
insights.so_what: Low direct market relevance; reflects a broader institutional-decline narrative among collapse-oriented thinkers.
